html:
In 1153 the king of the Maldives, a chain of coral islands southwest of India, became a Muslim, and his people followed. Before this the islands were Buddhist.

Maldivian tradition says the conversion came through a Muslim visitor, usually named as Abu al-Barakat, who freed the islanders from a sea demon that demanded a girl each month. The king took the title Sultan Muhammad al-Adil, and a line of sultans ruled the islands until 1968.

The real background was trade. The Maldives sat on the sea lanes between Arabia, India and Southeast Asia, and Muslim merchants dominated those lanes in this period of Indian Ocean trade. The islands exported cowrie shells, used as money as far away as West Africa and Bengal.

The traveller Ibn Battuta lived there in the 1340s and served as a judge. The Buddhist past left ruins under later mosques. Islam remains the state religion, and the Maldives is one of the few places in South Asia where the whole population is Muslim.
sum: In 1153 the king of the Maldives, a chain of coral islands southwest of India, became a Muslim, and his people followed. Before this the islands were Buddhist.
